t: Divisible Game — Kadane over Candidate Moduli
o: Alice picks an integer $k>1$ and a contiguous subarray $[l,r]$. Element $nums[i]$ contributes $+nums[i]$ if $k$ divides it, otherwise $-nums[i]$. She maximizes the subarray sum of these signed values, breaking ties on $k$ by taking the smallest. For a fixed $k$, the sign pattern is fixed, so the best $[l,r]$ is just the classic maximum (non-empty) subarray sum — Kadane's algorithm. Example 1: with $k=2$, indices 1..3 all become positive, giving 18, so the answer is $18\times2=36$. Example 2: $k=2$ turns the array into $[+2,-1,+2]$ whose best subarray is the whole array, worth 3, giving 6. Example 3: with $nums=[1]$ every $k$ makes the element negative; the least-bad choice is the smallest allowed $k=2$, yielding $-2 \equiv 10^9+5$. Constraints ($n\le1000$, $nums[i]\le10^6$) mean trying every $k$ up to $10^6$ is too slow, but the sign pattern only changes when $k$ crosses a divisor of some element — so only $O(n\cdot\tau(V))$ candidate values of $k$ matter.
k: For a fixed k, the problem reduces to maximum non-empty subarray sum of the array b[i] = nums[i] if k|nums[i] else -nums[i], solvable with Kadane in O(n).
The sign pattern for k only changes at divisors of the nums[i]; therefore only k values that divide some element (plus the smallest k that divides none) need to be tested.
The smallest k producing an 'nothing is divisible' pattern is found by scanning k = 2, 3, ... until no element is divisible; this scan terminates quickly because each visited k divides some element.
Kadane must consider non-empty subarrays (l <= r is mandatory), so an all-negative transformed array yields the largest single element negated.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute force over every k
a.i: Try every k from 2 to max(nums)+1 (any larger k behaves identically to max(nums)+1 since nothing is divisible). For each k, transform the array to signed values and run Kadane to get the best difference. Track the maximum difference and, on ties, the smallest k. This is simple and obviously correct, but at $O(n \cdot V)$ with $V=10^6$ it is too slow for the worst case in slower languages.
s: Let V = max(nums). Iterate k from 2 to V+1.
For each k, build the signed array b[i] = nums[i] if k divides nums[i] else -nums[i].
Run non-empty Kadane on b to get the best difference for this k.
Keep the global maximum difference; update the stored k only on a strict improvement (this keeps the smallest tied k automatically since k increases).
a.t: O(n * V) where V = max(nums) — for each of the V candidate k values we scan the array once.
a.sp: O(1) extra space — only running Kadane variables are kept.

a.i: The signed pattern for a given k depends only on which elements k divides, and this pattern is constant between consecutive 'interesting' values of k. Every interesting k either divides some nums[i] (so it is a divisor ≥ 2 of some element) or divides nothing (and the smallest such k is found by scanning upward from 2 — the scan only steps through values that divide something, so it is short). Evaluating only these candidates with Kadane gives the exact same answer as the brute force, since within each constant-pattern interval the smallest representative is included.
s: Collect all divisors d >= 2 of every nums[i] by trial division up to sqrt(nums[i]) into a set of candidates.
Find the smallest k >= 2 that divides no element (scan k = 2, 3, ... while some element is divisible by k) and add it to the candidates.
For each candidate k, run non-empty Kadane on b[i] = nums[i] if k|nums[i] else -nums[i]; keep the max difference, updating the stored k only on strict improvement.
a.t: O(n*sqrt(V) + C*n) where C is the number of distinct candidate k values (at most about n * tau(V) ~ 2.4e5 in the absolute worst case, typically far fewer) — divisor enumeration dominates collection, Kadane dominates evaluation.
a.sp: O(C) for the candidate set of k values.

w: In an interview, lead with the observation that fixing k reduces everything to maximum subarray sum, then immediately point out that only divisor-based candidates for k matter — that jump from $O(nV)$ to roughly $O(n\sqrt{V} + Cn)$ is the crux of the problem. Pitfalls: forgetting that the subarray must be non-empty (use Kadane initialized with -infinity, not the empty-subarray variant); forgetting that k need not divide any element (Example 3 requires the smallest 'divides-nothing' k, which is not always 2 — e.g. nums=[9] needs k=2 checked even though 3 is a divisor); mishandling negative results modulo 1e9+7 in C++/Java. Edge cases: single element, all-equal elements, arrays where the optimum is negative. Follow-ups: what if l and r had to span the whole array (then it is just total signed sum), or if Bob also chose adaptively (game-theory twist requiring minimax DP).
